title: Choral evensong
hook: a sung service at dusk, with the Magnificat and Nunc Dimittis

segments.voice: Yesterday, morning and evening: the prayer book's two hinges of the day. Your line was morning and evening. Did you mark both ends, even with one line each? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

The light is going outside a stone chapel. A few people sit in the carved wooden stalls: a student with a backpack, someone still in work clothes, a visitor who wandered in out of the cold. A bell, an organ note, and the choir begins. You can sing along if you know it. You can also just sit. The choir carries most of the singing: the psalm for the day, a song after each of the two readings, prayers sung back and forth, and then out into the dark. It's yesterday's Evening Prayer, the same bones, set to music. The English gave it an old, plain name. Today's word: evensong.

The two songs at the center of evensong come from the first pages of Luke's Gospel, and they belong to two people at opposite ends of a story. The first is Mary's. She has just been told she will bear a child, and she goes to visit her cousin Elizabeth. There she says: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." Listen to where it goes: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." That's not a lullaby. It's a world turned over. In church it's known by its first word in Latin, Magnificat. The second song is Simeon's. Luke says it had been shown to him that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord's Christ. When Mary and Joseph bring the baby into the temple, Simeon takes him in his arms and blesses God: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." Its Latin name is its first words, Nunc dimittis: now you let go. So evensong sets a beginning and an ending side by side. A woman carrying a child, singing about the low lifted up. A man who has waited, ready to go in peace. Sung at dusk, Simeon's words can be heard as a word about the day itself: the old man has seen what he waited for, and now he can let go. And these songs aren't only Anglican. Catholic evening prayer, Vespers, sings the Magnificat too.
screen: `A BEGINNING AND AN ENDING AT DUSK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen. If you can, play a recording of evensong, or just Simeon's song, and let it fill the room. If not, sit in the quiet and let one line come back by itself: now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace. Then let the day go, one piece at a time: the meeting, the drive, the dishes, the thing somebody said. You don't have to sing. Listening is allowed to be the whole prayer. If you pray, you can hand the day back to God in Simeon's words. The bell holds the time.
Evensong. Evening Prayer sung at dusk, with Mary's Magnificat and Simeon's Nunc dimittis at its heart.
Your line: the day ends in song. Tonight, end with one sung or hummed thing: a hymn, a psalm, a line you half remember. Let that be the last word of the day. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Choral evensong is sung by choirs in Anglican cathedrals, college chapels and some parish churches, usually in the late afternoon; people may join in the responses or simply sit and listen.

notes: The hook's scene (stone chapel, stalls, a few people) is illustrative, not a claim about any particular place or about attendance.
'Prayers sung on a single note' describes the sung responses and collects (monotone or plainsong settings vary by choir); confirm or soften.
'Nunc dimittis: now you let go' glosses the Latin 'nunc dimittis' (now you dismiss / let depart). Confirm the gloss; Magnificat glossed '(my soul) magnifies'.
Luke does not give Simeon's or Mary's age; the script avoids 'old man' and 'young mother' deliberately.
'Catholic evening prayer, Vespers, sings the Magnificat too': true of the Roman Liturgy of the Hours; confirm wording. Not ranked against Anglican use.
Practice suggests playing a recording; no specific recording or broadcast is named.

Editor pass: 'prayers sung on a single note' (uncertain, varies by choir) changed to 'prayers sung back and forth'; 'There she sings' changed to 'There she says', since Luke 1:46 reads 'And Mary said'.

Audit (2026-10-02): hook said the choir 'carries' the readings (readings are read, not sung); now 'most of the singing ... a song after each of the two readings'. The narrator's first-person gloss on the Nunc dimittis ('I've seen enough of God's goodness today') reworded as how the words can be heard, tied to Simeon.
